@graph.headline: AI agents need access—not a copy of your password
@graph.description: Credential brokers, separate identities and local AI each address different boundaries, not every security risk.

mainEntity.name: Should I give an AI agent my account password?

acceptedAnswer.text: Avoid copying a reusable password into an agent prompt or configuration when a product offers a more controlled authorization method. A password broker or a separate account may reduce some kinds of exposure, but neither is automatically safe. Check the requested permissions, identity, approval context, logging and revocation before connecting an account.

mainEntity.name: Is a separate agent account safer than a password broker?

acceptedAnswer.text: They solve different problems. A separate account can make the acting identity visible and easier to scope. A broker can mediate sign-in without revealing the underlying password, according to its vendor. Either design can still be over-permissioned or poorly monitored. Compare the actual scopes, audit trail, approval and revocation controls.

mainEntity.name: Does local AI keep all my information private?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not by itself. Running a model locally changes where inference happens, but it does not automatically define what a website or extension can read, what data it sends elsewhere, or which account permissions apply. Check the specific feature’s data-flow disclosures and permissions rather than assuming “local” means every part of the workflow stays on-device.

mainEntity.name: What does an approval screen need to show?

acceptedAnswer.text: A useful approval should make the acting identity, destination, requested action and scope understandable before the user agrees. It should also make it possible to decline and later revoke access. A generic confirmation without meaningful context may not support an informed choice, even if a product includes a human approval step.

mainEntity.name: Are the announced products independently security-tested?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cited launch posts describe vendor products and claims; they are not independent assessments of every configuration or integration. NIST, Google’s OAuth guidance and OWASP provide general security principles, not audits of these products. Look for published third-party evaluations, scope details, incident response and revocation evidence before treating a feature as assurance.
